units.title: Your Starter Pack
units.desc: The words you already know, corrected and in proper Jyutping

ex.en: Why?
How do I go?

words.note: Short, everyday form of 乜嘢 mat1 je5.

ex.en: What do you want?
What is this?
Where is your home?
Which one do you like?

words.note: Polite version of 邊個, e.g. on the phone.

ex.en: Who is it, please?
My big brother likes running.
My little sister is sleeping.

words.note: Means 'home'. A house as a building is 屋 uk1.

ex.en: I'm going home now.

words.en: week; day of the week (+ number)
words.note: 星期一 Monday … 星期六 Saturday, 星期日 Sunday.

ex.en: Today is Monday.

words.note: Many people drop the h: 'o2 ji5'.

ex.en: Can I use it?
I want to sleep.

ex.en: What are you doing?

ex.en: Give me a napkin, please.

words.note: Not the same as 鹹 haam4 (salty): -ng vs -m ending.

ex.en: Let's walk.
I'm going shopping with my big sister.
Pork and beef.

words.note: 同 alone = 'with'. 同埋 = 'and / together with'.
Sugar itself is 糖 tong4.
Many Hongkongers say 'laan4' (n→l). Both are understood.

ex.en: Cantonese is very difficult!

words.note: 落雨 = to rain; 緊 = -ing. There is no 'I' in it.
Often said 'au4 juk6' without the ng-.
Alone it's usually jyu2; in compounds jyu4 (e.g. 魚蛋 jyu4 daan2).

sentences.en: My family
Why are you sleeping now?
I like riding my bike.
Where is my little brother?
It's raining, I don't want to go running.
Can I use your computer?
This fish is very salty.
How do you use this appliance?
My big sister likes sweet things.
Who wants pork?
I walk home.
What day is it today?

grammar.title: Questions go where the answer goes
grammar.explain: Cantonese doesn't move question words to the front. Say the statement and drop 邊度 / 咩 / 邊個 into the slot of the answer.

examples.en: My home is in Geneva. → Where is your home?

grammar.title: 想 vs 想要
grammar.explain: 想 + verb = want to do. 想要 + thing = want a thing.

dialogue.title: At home on a rainy day

lines.en: What are you doing?
I'm watching TV.
Do you want to go running?
It's raining. I don't want to.
Then let's go shopping!
OK! Where to?

questions.q: What is B doing at first?
Why doesn't B want to go running?
What do they decide to do?

units.title: Sounds & Tones
units.desc: Hear and tell apart the 6 tones, and read Jyutping

words.note: Tone 1 · high and flat, like holding a high note.
Tone 2 · starts low-mid and rises, like a surprised 'eh?'.
Tone 3 · mid and flat, your normal speaking pitch.
Tone 4 · low and falling, the bottom of your voice.
Tone 5 · low with a small rise.
Tone 6 · low and flat, just under tone 3.
Ends in -t: short and clipped. Tone 1 height.
Ends in -t, tone 3 height.
Ends in -k, tone 6 height.
Same syllable as 食 sik6 but high — tones change meaning!
Ends in -p: close your lips without releasing.
Short a. Compare 街 gaai1.
Long aa. Compare 雞 gai1.
eo ≈ the 'eu' in French 'peur', then a short i.
oe ≈ French 'eu' in 'heure'. c = 'ts'.
ng- at the start, like the end of 'sing'. Many say 'o5'.
yu ≈ French 'u' in 'tu'.

sentences.en: Ten, eight, six, one.
I want to try.
I know how to eat with chopsticks.

grammar.title: Six tones, one chart
grammar.explain: Pitch is part of the word. Imagine your voice range as 5 steps: tone 1 sits at the top (5), tone 3 in the middle (3), tone 6 just below (2), tone 4 drops to the bottom (1). Tones 2 and 5 rise. Every Jyutping syllable ends with its tone number.

examples.en: poem, history, try, time, market, matter

grammar.title: Reading Jyutping
grammar.explain: j = English y · z ≈ dz · c ≈ ts · yu = French u · eo / oe ≈ French eu · aa is long, a is short · syllables ending -p, -t, -k are cut short.

units.title: Hello & Thanks
units.desc: Greet people, say thanks and sorry, and answer yes or no

words.note: Fine with strangers. Friends often just say the person's name, or 早晨 in the morning.

ex.en: Hello, I'm Ka-ming.

words.note: Used until about 11 a.m. There is no common 'good afternoon' — just say 你好.

ex.en: Good morning, Mr Chan!

words.note: Literally 'rest early'. Said when going to bed or leaving late at night — not 'good evening'.

ex.en: Good night, little sister!

words.note: From English 'bye-bye'; the most common goodbye in Hong Kong.

ex.en: Bye! See you on Monday!

words.note: A bit more formal than 拜拜.

ex.en: Goodbye, Mr Chan.

words.note: Use it when someone does something for you, to call a waiter, or to get past people. 唔該晒 = thanks a lot.

ex.en: Excuse me, where's the toilet?

words.note: For gifts, compliments and invitations. 多謝晒 = thanks very much.

ex.en: Thank you for your present!

words.note: Literally 'no need to thank'. The reply to 多謝 is 唔使客氣 m4 sai2 haak3 hei3.
A real apology. For small things (interrupting, saying no) use 唔好意思.

ex.en: Sorry! Are you OK?
Sorry, I can't go.
Never mind, I'll walk home.
No problem, go ahead and use it.

words.note: Links two nouns (I am Ka-ming). Alone, 係啊 hai6 aa3 means 'yes, that's right'.

ex.en: I'm Ka-ming.
No, I'm not Mr Chan.

words.note: 好 + adjective = very: 好甜 very sweet. 好啊！ = OK, sure!

ex.en: OK! Let's go!

words.note: Textbook phrase. Hongkongers more often say 最近點啊？ or 你好唔好啊？
Literally 'lately how?'. The everyday 'how are you'.

ex.en: Mr Chan, how have you been?

words.note: 幾 before an adjective = 'quite'. 都幾好 = actually quite good.

ex.en: Not bad. And you?
My big brother is called Ka-ming.

words.note: Polite opener before a question to a stranger.

ex.en: Excuse me, are you Mr Chan?

words.note: 得唔得？ = Is that OK? Answer 得 (yes) or 唔得 (no).

ex.en: Sure, no problem!

sentences.en: Good morning, Mr Chan! How have you been?
Pretty good, thanks.
Excuse me, are you Ka-ming?
No, I'm his big brother.
Sorry, I don't eat beef.
Never mind, no problem!
Is Saturday OK for you?
Good night! I'm going to sleep now.
Bye-bye! See you on Sunday!
Thank you! I really like it!
Excuse me, can I use the computer?
Is your big sister well?
This isn't sweet, it's salty!

grammar.title: 唔該 or 多謝?
grammar.explain: 唔該 thanks someone for doing something for you (a service, a small favour) and also means 'excuse me'. 多謝 thanks someone for a gift, a compliment or an invitation.

examples.en: Excuse me, I'd like a glass of water.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions: A-唔-A
grammar.explain: Repeat the verb with 唔 in the middle: 係唔係, 鍾唔鍾意. There's no single word for 'yes' or 'no' — answer with the verb (係 / 鍾意) or its negative (唔係 / 唔鍾意).

grammar.title: 好 = very
grammar.explain: Before an adjective, 好 means 'very' (好難, 好甜). On its own, 好 means 'good' or 'OK'.

lines.en: Oops, sorry!
It's fine. Oh, Ka-ming, good morning!
Good morning, Mr Chan! How have you been?
Pretty good, thanks. Where are you going?
I'm going running.
But it's raining!
No problem! I like running in the rain!
Haha, OK then, bye!
Bye!

questions.q: How has Mr Chan been?
Where is Ka-ming going?
What's the weather like?
What time of day is it?

units.title: About Me
units.desc: Say who you are, where you're from, where you live and what languages you speak

words.note: Many Hongkongers drop the ng-: 'o5'. Both are fine.

ex.en: I'm Mark.

words.note: Often said 'lei5' (n→l). The polite 您 is almost never used in Cantonese.

ex.en: And you?

words.note: One word for he, she and it — no gender in speech.

ex.en: She doesn't speak French.
We live in Geneva.
Are you (all) French?
They aren't Swiss.

words.note: Literally 'fragrant harbour'. 香港人 = a Hongkonger.

ex.en: I was born in Hong Kong.
Do you like Switzerland?

words.note: Literally 'new west orchid' — a sound-and-meaning blend of 'New Zealand'.

ex.en: I'm a New Zealander.
My big sister lives in France.

words.note: 英國 jing1 gwok3 = the UK, 美國 mei5 gwok3 = the USA. 國 = country.

ex.en: Where in Geneva do you live?

words.note: 住喺 + place = live in. 喺 hai2 is 'at / in'.

ex.en: Where do you live?

words.en: to know how to; to know (a person)
words.note: 識講 = can speak. 我識佢 = I know him.

ex.en: Do you know him?
Please speak slowly.

words.note: 話 is waa2 here (tone change). Also 廣東話 = 'the speech of Guangdong'.

ex.en: Can you speak Cantonese?

words.note: 文 man2 with a tone change. For languages, 文 is used for 'written / national' language: 英文, 法文, 中文.

ex.en: My mum doesn't speak English.
Is French difficult?
I speak a little Cantonese.

words.note: In speech 名 is meng2: 你叫咩名啊？ (What's your name?). The formal word 名字 is ming4 zi6.

ex.en: What's your name?

words.note: 幾多歲 = how old? No verb needed: 佢八歲 = he is eight.

ex.en: How old is your little sister?

words.note: 結咗婚 = married. 未結婚 = not married (yet).

ex.en: Is your big brother married?

sentences.en: I'm from Hong Kong. And you?
I'm a New Zealander, but I was born in Hong Kong.
We now live in Switzerland.
I can speak a little Cantonese.
Can she speak English?
My little brother can't speak French.
Are they Chinese?
No, they're Swiss.
What's his name?
How old are you this year?
My big sister is married; my little sister isn't married yet.
Cantonese is hard, English isn't.
Do you (all) like living in Geneva?

grammar.title: 係 + place + 人 = nationality
grammar.explain: Add 人 jan4 (person) after a place to say where someone is from: 香港人, 瑞士人, 法國人. To ask, put 邊度 in the place slot: 你係邊度人啊？

grammar.title: 哋 makes pronouns plural
grammar.explain: 我 → 我哋 (we), 你 → 你哋 (you all), 佢 → 佢哋 (they). Only pronouns take 哋, not nouns.

examples.en: Do they live in Hong Kong?

grammar.title: 住喺 = live in
grammar.explain: 喺 hai2 means 'at / in'. Put it between the verb and the place: 住喺日內瓦. Don't confuse it with 係 hai6 (to be).

lines.en: Hello! Did you just move in?
Yes, my name's Mark. I live on the third floor.
I'm Yan, from the fifth floor. Oh, you speak Cantonese?
Just a little. I was born in Hong Kong.
So you're a Hongkonger?
I'm a New Zealander, but my family are all Hongkongers.
Wow, you speak really well!
Thanks! Do you speak French?
Not a word! Come up for a cup of tea when you're free!
Sure, thanks! Bye!

questions.q: Which floor does Mark live on?
Where was Mark born?
What nationality is Mark?
Does Yan speak French?

units.title: Numbers & Money
units.desc: Count, give phone numbers, ask prices and haggle at a market stall

words.note: Inside a number, 零 fills an empty place: 一百零五 = 105.

ex.en: It's 105 dollars.
One char siu bao, please!

words.note: Use 二 when counting and in bigger numbers (十二, 二十). Before a measure word, 'two' is 兩.

ex.en: Two plus two is four.
My little brother is three.

words.note: Sounds like 死 sei2 (to die), so 4 is unlucky — many HK buildings skip the 4th floor.

ex.en: There are four of us.

words.note: A syllable with no vowel: just hum 'ng' with a low rising tone.

ex.en: This one is five dollars.
My big sister is sixteen.
A week has seven days.

words.note: Lucky! It rhymes with 發 faat3 (to get rich).

ex.en: This car is 880,000 dollars.

words.note: 九 also sounds like 久 (long-lasting) — another lucky number.

ex.en: It's ninety-nine dollars, not expensive.

words.note: Careful: 十 sap6 (ten) vs 四 sei3 (four). Keep the -p closed at the end of sap6.

ex.en: Three for ten dollars!

words.note: 一百五 or just 百五 = 150 (the last zero is dropped).

ex.en: This one is 150 dollars.
This computer is 8,000 dollars.
Ten thousand dollars? I don't want it!

words.note: 兩 + measure word: 兩個, 兩張, 兩蚊. Never 二個.

ex.en: Two napkins, please.

words.note: Numbers and 呢/嗰 need a measure word before a noun. 個 is the default one: 一個人, 呢個.

ex.en: I want that one.
How many do you want?

words.note: 錢 is cin2 in speech. Shorter: 幾錢 gei2 cin2.

ex.en: How much is this?

words.note: The spoken word for dollar. Written price tags say 元, but nobody says it.

ex.en: A cup of milk tea is twenty dollars.

words.note: 五毫子 = 50 cents. With dollars, people just say 個: 兩個半 = $2.50, 三個二 = $3.20.

ex.en: Fifty cents? So cheap!

words.note: In the sense 'cheap', 平 is peng4. (ping4 is 'flat / peaceful', as in 和平.)

ex.en: The oranges aren't cheap.
Is it expensive?

sentences.en: How much is the bicycle?
Three hundred dollars? So expensive!
It's not expensive, it's really cheap!
Two char siu bao, please.
My big brother is twenty-five.
My phone number is 9123 4567.
This pack of tissues is $2.50.
How much is beef per catty?
My little sister came first in the race.
Is this your first time in Switzerland?
Give me two, please.
Switzerland is so expensive — a coffee costs fifty (HK) dollars!
How many computers do you have at home?

grammar.title: Building numbers 11–99
grammar.explain: Just stack them: 十一 = 10+1, 二十 = 2×10, 二十五 = 25. In speech, 二十 + digit is usually shortened to 廿 jaa6: 廿五 = 25.

grammar.title: 兩 vs 二
grammar.explain: 'Two' of something (before a measure word like 個, 張, 蚊) is 兩. Inside bigger numbers and when counting, use 二: 十二個, 二十蚊.

grammar.title: Saying prices the HK way
grammar.explain: With cents, drop 蚊 and say 個: 個半 = $1.50, 三個二 = $3.20. With hundreds, drop the last zero: 百五 = 150, 三百二 = 320.

dialogue.title: Buying fruit at a market stall

lines.en: Boss, how much are the oranges?
Three for ten dollars.
That cheap? I'll take six.
Six, that's twenty. Want some apples too?
How much is an apple?
Eight dollars each.
Eight dollars? That's expensive! No thanks.
OK then, five for thirty. Deal?
Deal! Fifty dollars altogether — here you go.
Thanks a lot!

questions.q: How much are the oranges?
How many oranges does A buy?
Why does A first say no to the apples?
How much does A pay in total?

units.title: Days & Time
units.desc: Tell the time, talk about today, tomorrow and yesterday, and make (or miss!) appointments

ex.en: It's raining today.

words.note: 聽 is ting1 here (as 'listen' it's teng1). In fast speech it often sounds like 'tim1 jat6'.

ex.en: See you tomorrow!

words.note: Also written 琴日 kam4 jat6 — same word, two pronunciations.

ex.en: Where did you go yesterday?

words.note: And 前日 cin4 jat6 = the day before yesterday.

ex.en: The day after tomorrow is my birthday.

words.note: Same as 星期 but more casual: 禮拜一 = Monday, 禮拜日 = Sunday.

ex.en: See you next week!
What time is it now?

words.note: In speech 鐘 is usually dropped: 三點 = three o'clock.

ex.en: It's three o'clock now.

words.note: 七點半 = 7:30. 半個鐘 = half an hour.

ex.en: I get up at half past seven.

words.note: Counts the numbers on a clock face: 三點三個字 = 3:15, 兩個字 = 10 minutes. Often just 三點三.

ex.en: He's ten minutes late.
Wait ten minutes for me, please.
I drink coffee in the morning.

words.note: Lunchtime and early afternoon. 下晝 haa6 zau3 = afternoon.

ex.en: Shall we go shopping this afternoon?
Don't drink coffee at night.
What do you want to eat tonight?

words.note: 早啲 = a bit earlier.

ex.en: You're so early today!

words.note: 遲啲 = later on. 遲咗 = (is) late.

ex.en: He came home very late today.
Sorry, I'm late!
I don't have time.
When are you going back to Hong Kong?

words.note: Months are numbered: 一月 January … 十二月 December. 下個月 = next month.

ex.en: I'm going to France next month.

words.note: 今年 this year, but 舊年 gau6 nin2 last year and 出年 ceot1 nin2 next year (tone change).

ex.en: I've lived in Geneva for three years.

words.note: Dates go big → small: 十一月四號 = 4 November.

ex.en: What's the date today?

sentences.en: Today is the 4th of November, a Wednesday.
What day is it tomorrow?
It's half past three now.
I'm going running tomorrow morning.
Do you have time tonight?
Sorry, I'm ten minutes late.
It rained all day yesterday.
We're going to Hong Kong the day after tomorrow!
I don't have time to watch TV.
When is your birthday?
I go to bed at eleven at night.
I'm not free next Saturday.
Is it too late? — No, it's still early!

grammar.title: Time comes before the verb
grammar.explain: Put 'when' right after the subject (or at the very start), never at the end: 我聽日去 = I'm going tomorrow. Bigger units come first: 聽日朝早七點.

examples.en: I'm going to Hong Kong tomorrow.
Tomorrow morning at seven, I go running.

grammar.title: Telling the time: 點, 半, 個字
grammar.explain: Hour + 點: 三點. Add 半 for half past: 三點半. Minutes are counted in 個字 (5-minute steps on the clock face): 三點三 = 3:15, 三點九 = 3:45. You can also say exact minutes with 分: 三點十分.

grammar.title: Days of the week
grammar.explain: 星期 or 禮拜 + number: 一 Monday … 六 Saturday. Sunday is 日 (not 七!): 星期日 / 禮拜日.

lines.en: Hello? Where are you? It's already half past three!
Sorry! I just got up.
What? It's the afternoon!
I only went to bed at two last night…
Sigh. What time will you get here?
Twenty minutes… no, half an hour!
OK, I'll wait half an hour. See you at four!
Thanks so much! Dinner's on me tonight!

questions.q: What time is it when A calls?
Why is B late?
When will they meet?
How does B make up for it?

units.title: Family & People
units.desc: Talk about your family, ask who's who in a photo, and say what you have (or don't)

words.note: Adults often say 阿爸 aa3 baa4 or the casual 老豆 lou5 dau6.

ex.en: My dad lives in Hong Kong.

words.note: Also 阿媽 aa3 maa1.

ex.en: Mum, I'm home!

words.note: The everyday word — not slangy at all.

ex.en: My husband doesn't eat lamb.
Is your wife Swiss?

words.note: Usually with 個: 我個仔 = my son. Also a 'little' suffix: 男仔 boy.

ex.en: My son is eight.

words.note: 'Daughter' is neoi2 (tone change): 我個女. 女 neoi5 on its own means 'female'.

ex.en: Does your daughter speak French?

words.note: Chinese has different words for each side of the family.

ex.en: Grandpa is ninety this year.
Grandma loves watching TV.
My grandpa doesn't speak English.

words.note: Also a polite way to address any elderly woman.

ex.en: Where does your grandma live?
He's my good friend.
Does she have a boyfriend?

words.note: Only for a romantic partner. A female friend is just 朋友.

ex.en: My little brother's girlfriend is French.
There are lots of people in Hong Kong.
Who's that boy?
Is that kid a boy or a girl?

words.note: The everyday word. 家庭 (u01) is more formal: 'the family unit'.

ex.en: My family are all in Hong Kong.

words.note: Polite and kind. A more casual word is 細路 sai3 lou6.

ex.en: The kids are sleeping.

words.note: Same as 哥哥 but more casual. Also 'boss / dude' in slang.

ex.en: My big brother is married.
I have two little sisters.

words.fr: ne pas avoir ; il n'y a pas
words.note: 冇 replaces 唔有, which doesn't exist. 有冇…？ = Do you have…?

ex.en: I don't have any brothers or sisters.

words.note: In a question: how many? In a statement: a few (我有幾個朋友 = I have a few friends).

ex.en: How many kids do you have?

sentences.en: How many people are there in your family?
Four: Dad, Mum, my big brother and me.
Do you have a girlfriend?
No, I don't.
I have a son and a daughter.
My wife and I live in Geneva.
My grandma is ninety and still very sprightly!
Is that your boyfriend?
No, he's my husband!
Dad doesn't have a car; he rides a bike.
My son likes playing video games, my daughter likes running.
Is there anyone at home?
I have a few Swiss friends.

grammar.title: 有 / 冇 / 有冇
grammar.explain: 有 = have / there is. The negative is 冇 (never 唔有). To ask, use 有冇: 你有冇車？ Answer 有 or 冇.

examples.en: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
Yes, I have a big sister.

grammar.title: 'My' without 嘅
grammar.explain: For family and close people, just put the pronoun in front: 我媽媽 (my mum), 你老公 (your husband). For 仔 and 女, add the measure word 個: 我個仔, 佢個女.

grammar.title: …嚟㗎 to identify someone
grammar.explain: 係 + noun + 嚟㗎 means 'is (actually) a…', used when explaining or correcting who/what something is. Very common in speech.

lines.en: Wow, so many people! Is this your family?
Yes. These two are my grandpa and grandma.
And who's this handsome guy? Your boyfriend?
No! That's my big brother!
Is he married?
Yes. That's his wife, and the two kids are theirs.
So cute! Boys or girls?
One boy, one girl. And do you have any brothers or sisters?
No, it's just me.

questions.q: Who is the handsome man in the photo?
Is the big brother married?
What children does the big brother have?
How many brothers and sisters does A have?

units.title: Getting Around
units.desc: Take the MTR, bus, minibus or taxi, ask the way and say where you are

words.note: No word for 'to' is needed: 去中環 = go to Central.

ex.en: Where are you going?

words.note: Also heard as lei4. The opposite of 去.

ex.en: My friend is coming to Hong Kong tomorrow.

words.note: Don't confuse with 係 hai6 'to be'. Only the tone differs.

ex.en: I'm at the airport.

words.en: to go back / return (to a usual place)
words.note: Used for places you belong to: 返屋企 go home, 返香港 go back to HK.

ex.en: She's gone back to Hong Kong.

words.note: 坐 co5 also works: 坐巴士. 坐 alone = to sit.

ex.en: I take the MTR home.

words.note: Official name 港鐵 gong2 tit3 (MTR). People say both 搭地鐵 and 搭港鐵.

ex.en: Where is the MTR station?

words.note: From English 'bus'. Bus stop = 巴士站.

ex.en: The bus stop is on the left.
Taking a taxi is expensive.

words.note: The 16-seat red or green minibuses. You shout your stop to the driver!

ex.en: Is there a minibus to the airport?

words.note: Plane = 飛機 fei1 gei1.

ex.en: How long does it take to get to the airport?

words.note: 地鐵站 MTR station, 巴士站 bus stop, 下個站 next stop.

ex.en: I'm getting off at the next stop.
Which exit should I take?

words.note: Turn left = 轉左 zyun3 zo2.

ex.en: The toilet is on the left.

words.note: Turn right = 轉右 zyun3 jau6.

ex.en: The bank is on the right.

words.note: 轉左 turn left, 轉右 turn right, 轉車 change trains/buses.

ex.en: Turn right at the second junction.
Go straight, then turn left.

words.note: Many people say 'gan6'. 好近 = very close.

ex.en: The MTR station is very close.
Is it far?

words.note: Answer with a duration: 十分鐘, 一個鐘.

ex.en: How long will you wait?

words.note: 到咗 = has arrived. 就到 = almost there.

ex.en: I've arrived!

words.note: Get on = 上車 soeng5 ce1.

ex.en: Where do we get off?

words.note: Shout it loudly before your stop. Add the place: 前面有落 = stop up ahead.

ex.en: Stop up ahead, please!

sentences.en: Excuse me, how do I get to Central?
Go straight, and turn left at the second junction.
The MTR station is close, it's only a five-minute walk.
It takes about forty minutes by bus.
Is Tsim Sha Tsui far from here?
Where are you? I'm at the bus stop.
To the airport, please. (to a taxi driver)
I walk home every day.
Do I need to change trains?
The airport isn't far, it's about half an hour.
When does your plane arrive?
We take the minibus to go up the hill.
Come to my place on Saturday!

grammar.title: No 'to': just verb + place
grammar.explain: 去, 嚟 and 返 take the place directly, with no word for 'to'. To say how you travel, put 搭 + transport before it.

examples.en: I take the MTR to the airport.

grammar.title: 喺 + place comes before the action
grammar.explain: 'Where' something happens goes before the verb, not at the end like in English: 'I at Central work', not 'I work at Central'.

grammar.title: How long? 要幾耐
grammar.explain: Ask 'how long does it take' with 要幾耐. Answer with 要 + duration; add 左右 or 大概 for 'about'.

examples.en: How long does it take to walk there?

dialogue.title: Asking the way to the MTR

lines.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the MTR station?
Go straight, and turn right at the second junction.
Is it far?
Not far, about five minutes on foot.
Actually I'm going to the airport. What should I take?
Take the airport bus, it's very convenient. The stop is just over there on the left.
How long does it take?
About an hour.
Thanks so much!
No problem.

questions.q: Where should A turn to reach the MTR station?
How far is the MTR station on foot?
What does B suggest for getting to the airport?
Where is the bus stop?

units.title: Shopping
units.desc: Point at things, ask for sizes and colours, pay and bargain at the market

words.note: Literally 'have-not-have'. Answer 有 (yes) or 冇 (no).

ex.en: Do you have a smaller size?

words.note: 呢 + classifier: 呢件 this (garment), 呢對 this pair.

ex.en: How much is this?

words.note: 嗰 go2 = that. 嗰件, 嗰對, 嗰度 (there).

ex.en: I want that one, not this one.

words.note: Plural: no classifier needed. 'Those' = 嗰啲 go2 di1.

ex.en: Are these on sale?

words.note: 試吓 si3 haa5 = have a try. Fitting room = 試身室.

ex.en: Can I try it on?
These shoes are too big.

words.note: Sizes: 細碼 S, 中碼 M, 大碼 L.

ex.en: This T-shirt is a bit small.

words.note: Classifier 件 gin6: 一件衫. Clothes in general = 衫 too.

ex.en: I want to buy a few tops.

words.note: Classifier 條 tiu4: 一條褲. Jeans = 牛仔褲.

ex.en: These trousers are too long.

words.note: Classifier 對 deoi3 (a pair). Trainers = 波鞋 bo1 haai4.

ex.en: I like that pair of shoes.
Do you have other colours?

words.note: Red is the lucky colour, especially at Chinese New Year.

ex.en: My mum likes red.

words.note: Also: 白色 baak6 sik1 white, 藍色 laam4 sik1 blue.

ex.en: Do you have it in black?

words.note: 平 'cheap' is said peng4 in everyday speech. 平啲啦 = come on, cheaper!

ex.en: Can you make it cheaper?

words.en: on sale; to reduce the price

ex.en: The shops are all having sales now.

words.note: Also written 俾錢. 'I'll pay' = 我畀.

ex.en: Where do I pay?

words.note: Many market stalls take cash only: 淨係收現金.

ex.en: Sorry, we only take cash.

words.en: to pay by card (swipe a card)
words.note: 碌 = to swipe/roll; 卡 is said kaat1 here, from English 'card'.

ex.en: Can I pay by card?

words.note: HK's stored-value card for the MTR, buses, shops. Top up = 增值 zang1 zik6.

ex.en: Do you take Octopus?
I go to the supermarket after work.

words.note: Grocery shopping for dinner = 買餸 maai5 sung3.

ex.en: The vegetables at the market are very fresh.

words.note: 唔夠錢 = not enough money. 夠唔夠 = is it enough?

ex.en: I don't have enough money.

sentences.en: Boss, how much is this top?
Do you have a bigger one?
This one is too expensive, that one is cheaper.
Do you have these trousers in black?
I'll take two of these.
Is a hundred dollars enough?
I forgot to bring cash, can I pay with Octopus?
This red one is really pretty!
The supermarket is having a big sale today.
My grandma goes to the wet market every morning.
I don't want a bag, thanks.
These shoes don't fit, they're too small.
Who's paying? — I'll pay!

grammar.title: 呢 / 嗰 + classifier + noun
grammar.explain: 'This' and 'that' need a classifier between them and the noun: 呢件衫 (this top), 嗰條褲 (those trousers), 呢對鞋 (this pair of shoes). For plurals use 啲: 呢啲衫 (these clothes).

examples.en: That pair of shoes is cheap.

grammar.title: Adjective + 啲 = a bit more
grammar.explain: Put 啲 after an adjective to mean '-er / a bit more': 平啲 cheaper, 大啲 bigger, 細啲 smaller. Very handy when bargaining.

examples.en: Do you have a smaller one?

grammar.title: 有冇…? and the A-not-A question
grammar.explain: 有冇 + thing asks 'do you have / is there'. Any verb or adjective can be doubled with 唔 to ask yes/no: 收唔收 (do you accept?), 夠唔夠 (enough?).

lines.en: Boss, how much is this bag?
Three hundred dollars.
Wow, so expensive! Can you go cheaper?
OK, two hundred and eighty.
Two hundred, come on. I'll pay cash.
No way… two fifty, that's the lowest.
Hmm… do you have it in black?
Yes! Here, have a look.
OK, two fifty. Can I use Octopus?
No, cash only!

questions.q: What was the first price?
What price do they agree on?
Which colour does A ask for?
How does A have to pay?

units.title: My Day
units.desc: Describe your daily routine and put actions in order: first, then, after that

words.note: Also 'to wake up' in everyday speech. Alarm clock = 鬧鐘 naau6 zung1.

ex.en: What time do you get up?

words.note: 刷 is caat3 here, not 'saat3'.

ex.en: Go brush your teeth!

words.note: Literally 'rinse cool'. Hongkongers usually shower at night.

ex.en: I'm showering, wait a moment.
I usually have breakfast at a cha chaan teng.

words.note: 返 again: work is a place you 'return' to every day.

ex.en: I take the MTR to work.

words.note: 收工 sau1 gung1 is also common, and is used as a cheerful 'done for the day!'

ex.en: What time do you finish work?

words.note: Finish school = 放學 fong3 hok6.

ex.en: My son goes to school at eight.

words.note: Very HK. 晏 = midday (晏晝).

ex.en: Shall we have lunch together?
Come to my place for dinner tonight.

words.note: Literally 'cook rice', but means cooking any meal.

ex.en: Who cooks at your home?
I cook, you wash the dishes.
I do the laundry on Sundays.

words.note: 執 = pick up / tidy. 執嘢 = pack your things.

ex.en: My room is so messy, I need to tidy up.

words.note: 食完 finish eating, 做完 finish doing, 洗完 finish washing.

ex.en: Have you finished eating?

words.note: 日日 jat6 jat6 means the same and is very colloquial.

ex.en: I go running every day.

words.note: 平時 ping4 si4 'normally' is used the same way.

ex.en: I usually get up at seven.

words.note: 先 goes before the first verb, 再 before the second.

ex.en: First take a shower, then eat.
I brush my teeth, then I shower.

words.note: Verb + 完 + 之後 = after doing: 食完飯之後.

ex.en: After work I go to the gym.

words.note: 一個鐘頭 = one hour; often shortened to 一個鐘.

ex.en: I work nine hours a day.

words.en: to leave the house, go out
words.note: Late = 遲到 ci4 dou3.

ex.en: I leave the house at eight every day.

sentences.en: I get up at seven every day.
First brush your teeth, then have breakfast.
I usually have lunch at one.
After work I go to the supermarket, then I go home and cook.
It takes me an hour to get to work.
I don't go to work on Saturdays.
Do you shower in the morning or at night?
My husband washes the dishes after dinner.
I'm rarely late for work.
On Sundays I tidy up and do the laundry.
The kids finish school at three-thirty.
I have to get up very early tomorrow, so I want to go to bed early tonight.

grammar.title: Time goes before the verb
grammar.explain: When something happens (每日, 七點, 星期六) comes before the verb, either right after the subject or at the very start.

examples.en: Every day I go to work by bus.

grammar.title: Ordering actions: 先…再…, 然後, 之後
grammar.explain: 先 A 再 B = first A, then B (often an instruction). 然後 links a list of steps. X 之後 = after X; use Verb + 完 + 之後 for 'after finishing'.

examples.en: Wash your hands first, then eat.
I get up, then brush my teeth, then shower.

grammar.title: Duration goes after the verb
grammar.explain: 'For how long' comes after the verb: 瞓咗八個鐘 (slept for eight hours). Compare with clock time, which comes before.

examples.en: He works ten hours a day.

lines.en: Hey! It's already eight-thirty, aren't you getting up?
What?! My alarm didn't ring!
Don't you start work at nine?
Yes! It takes me forty minutes to get there. I'm going to be late!
Brush your teeth first, then leave. Skip the shower.
What about breakfast?
Here's a pineapple bun, eat it on the MTR.
Thanks! I'll cook dinner tonight!

questions.q: What time is it when A wakes B?
Why did B oversleep?
What does A tell B to skip?
What will B do to say thanks?

units.title: Home & Gadgets
units.desc: Talk about your flat, switch things on and off, and get broken things fixed

words.note: Said fong2 on its own. Classifier 間: 一間房. Bedroom = 睡房.

ex.en: My room is very small.

words.note: Flats are described as 兩房一廳 'two bedrooms, one living room'.

ex.en: The kids are watching TV in the living room.

words.note: Many people say ceoi4 fong2.

ex.en: Mum is cooking in the kitchen.

words.note: In HK flats the toilet and shower are usually in one room, all called 廁所.

ex.en: Excuse me, where's the toilet?
Can I open the window? It's so stuffy.
Remember to shut the door when you go out.

words.note: 開門 open the door, 開燈 turn on the light, 開冷氣 turn on the air-con.

ex.en: It's so hot, turn on the air-con!

words.en: to close / shut; to switch off
words.note: A very Cantonese character: a bar across a door. 閂燈 = turn off the light.

ex.en: Turn off the light before you sleep.
It's too dark, please turn on the light.

words.note: The machine is 冷氣機, but people just say 部冷氣.

ex.en: The air-con in the office is too strong.

words.note: Literally 'snow cupboard'.

ex.en: Is there any beer in the fridge?
The washing machine is so noisy.
My phone's battery is dead.

words.note: Everyday word. 充電 cung1 din6 is the written/formal one.

ex.en: Can I charge my phone here?

words.note: 壞 = bad/broken, 咗 = it has happened.

ex.en: My computer is broken.

words.note: 整返好 = fix it back to working. Also 'make': 整嘢食 = make food.

ex.en: Do you know how to fix it?

words.en: repairman; (polite address to a tradesman or driver)
words.note: Call taxi drivers, chefs and repairmen 師傅.

ex.en: Sir, when can you come and fix it?

words.note: Classifier 條: 一條鎖匙.

ex.en: I can't find my key!

words.en: classifier: flat things (tables, beds, paper, tickets)

ex.en: This table is very heavy.
I want to buy a new phone.
He bought a new car.
That restaurant is really good.

sentences.en: My flat has two bedrooms and a living room.
The toilet is next to the kitchen.
The air-con is broken!
Remember to turn off the lights when you go out.
My phone is dead, I need to charge it.
Can you fix computers?
There are three phones on the table.
Don't open the window, it's raining.
The key is in the kitchen.
There's nothing in the fridge.
When will the repairman come?
Which room is yours?

grammar.title: Classifier + noun = 'the'
grammar.explain: Drop 呢/嗰 and a classifier alone in front of a noun means 'the (one we both know)': 部冷氣 = the air-con, 條鎖匙 = the key. English needs 'the' or 'my'; Cantonese just uses the classifier.

grammar.title: Choosing the classifier
grammar.explain: 部 for machines, 張 for flat things, 架 for vehicles, 間 for rooms and buildings, 條 for long thin things (keys, trousers, fish). If you're unsure, 個 is the safe default.

examples.en: I have a computer and a bike.
There are two beds in this room.

grammar.title: 開 and 閂: open/close, on/off
grammar.explain: The same verbs work for doors, windows and devices: 開 = open / switch on, 閂 = close / switch off.

lines.en: Oh no, the air-con is broken!
What? It's thirty-four degrees today!
It's on, but it's not cold at all.
Have you tried turning it off and on again?
I tried, it still doesn't work.
Then call the repairman to come and fix it.
The repairman says he can't come until tomorrow.
Ugh, how are we going to sleep tonight?
Open the windows and turn on the fan!
Forget it, I'm sleeping at my friend's place!

questions.q: What's wrong with the air-con?
How hot is it today?
When can the repairman come?
What does B decide to do?

units.title: Weather & Feelings
units.desc: Talk about the weather, typhoons and rain, and say how you feel

ex.en: How's the weather today?
Hong Kong's summer is really hot.

words.note: Used for weather, food and drinks: 凍檸茶 = iced lemon tea. 凍親 = catch a chill.

ex.en: Is it cold in Switzerland?

words.note: Nice and cool. Compare 凍 = cold.

ex.en: It's lovely and cool in autumn.

words.note: The classic HK summer feeling. 好焗 means the same.

ex.en: It's so muggy today, it's probably going to rain.

words.en: to be sunny (the sun comes out)

ex.en: The sun's out, let's go to the beach!

words.note: Like 落雨 'to rain': things 'fall'. It never snows in Hong Kong!

ex.en: It's snowing in Geneva!

words.note: Literally 'wind strikes'. Typhoon signal = 風球; No. 8 = 八號風球, schools and offices close.

ex.en: There's a typhoon tomorrow, we don't have to go to work.

words.note: Classifier 把 baa2. 帶遮 = take an umbrella.

ex.en: Remember to take an umbrella.

words.note: 覺得 + adjective = to feel …; also 'I think that …'.

ex.en: I feel a bit cold.

words.note: 唔開心 = unhappy, upset.

ex.en: Why are you so happy today?

words.note: A very Cantonese character. 好攰 = so tired.

ex.en: I worked ten hours today, I'm so tired.

words.note: Literally 'neck thirsty'.

ex.en: I'm thirsty, I want an iced lemon tea.

words.note: Colloquial reading geng1. 唔使驚 = don't be afraid.

ex.en: My daughter is scared of thunder.

words.note: 嬲咗 = has got angry. 唔好嬲 = don't be angry.

ex.en: Is your wife angry?

words.note: 好悶 = so boring / I'm so bored.

ex.en: Staying home all day is so boring.
I have an exam tomorrow, I'm so nervous.
Don't worry, I'm fine.

words.note: 唔舒服 = unwell, not feeling good.

ex.en: I'm not feeling well, I want to go home.

words.note: Signals 1, 3, 8, 9, 10. 掛八號風球 = hoist signal No. 8: offices and schools close. Luckily = 好彩 hou2 coi2.

ex.en: Will they hoist the No. 8 signal tonight?

sentences.en: It's very hot today, thirty-three degrees.
It's raining, did you bring an umbrella?
Is there going to be a typhoon tomorrow?
The Observatory has hoisted the No. 8 signal.
I think Hong Kong's winter isn't cold at all.
Are you tired? Do you want to rest for a bit?
He's not happy because he lost his phone.
Don't be angry, it's my fault.
It's snowing in Switzerland now, and the sun's out in Hong Kong.
This sofa is really comfortable.
Luckily it didn't rain today.
Are you scared? — No, I'm not scared.

grammar.title: Adjectives are verbs: no 'to be'
grammar.explain: Never put 係 before an adjective. Use 好 (very / just linking) instead: 我好攰 = I'm tired. Without 好 it sounds like a contrast.

grammar.title: 有啲 = a bit (for feelings)
grammar.explain: 有啲 + adjective = 'a bit / rather', usually for something negative: 有啲凍, 有啲攰. 一啲都唔 + adjective = 'not at all'.

examples.en: This film isn't boring at all.

grammar.title: 會 = will / likely to
grammar.explain: 會 wui5 before a verb is used for predictions, especially about the weather: 會落雨 = it's going to rain. Ask with 會唔會 (often said wui6 m4 wui5).

lines.en: Hey, the No. 8 signal is up! No work today!
Yay! I'm so happy!
But the wind is really strong outside. Are you scared?
A little. Have you closed the windows?
All closed. Is there any food in the fridge?
Only instant noodles… and two beers.
Good enough! Let's watch TV at home.
Wait… the Observatory says it'll go down to No. 3 at two o'clock.
Oh no… so we still have to go to work in the afternoon?
Yep! How annoying!

questions.q: Why don't they have to go to work in the morning?
options: The No. 8 typhoon signal is up
Their office is closed for repairs

questions.q: What food do they have at home?
What happens at two o'clock?
options: The signal goes down to No. 3
The signal goes up to No. 10

questions.q: How do they feel at the end?

units.title: Grammar Power-ups
units.desc: The small words that make Cantonese sound natural: aspect markers, particles and linkers

words.en: (after verb) completed action: did / has done
words.note: Goes right after the verb: 食咗 ate, 買咗 bought. Negative: 冇 + verb (no 咗).

ex.en: I've eaten already.

words.note: 睇緊 watching, 做緊 doing. With verb-object words it splits them: 沖緊涼, 瞓緊覺.

ex.en: I'm cooking, I can't talk right now.

words.note: 去過 = have been to. Negative: 未 + verb + 過 = have never (yet) done.

ex.en: Have you ever been to Japan?

words.fr: pas encore ; (en fin de question) … déjà ?
words.note: Question: 你食咗飯未啊？ Answer: 食咗 (yes) or 未啊 / 仲未 (not yet).

ex.en: Have you had lunch yet?

words.en: (end of sentence) new situation: now / already
words.fr: (fin de phrase) nouvelle situation : ça y est
words.note: Marks a change: 落雨喇 'it's (started) raining now'. Often with 咗: 到咗喇.

ex.en: It's ten o'clock already, I'm going.

words.en: (end of sentence) suggestion / request: let's, come on
words.note: Softens orders and makes suggestions: 食啦 'go on, eat'. Don't confuse with 喇 laa3 (change).

ex.en: Let's go together!

words.en: (end of sentence) softener; makes questions friendly
words.note: Without it many questions sound blunt. Also written 呀, but 啊 is the standard here.

ex.en: Where are you going?

words.en: (end of sentence) that's how it is (explaining / emphasising)
words.note: 嘅 + 啊 merged. Gives a reason or a fact: 好貴㗎! In questions it shows surprise: 係你㗎？

ex.en: Taxis in Hong Kong are cheap, you know.

words.en: (end of sentence) passing on news / 'oh, by the way'
words.note: Used for something you just noticed or heard: 佢話唔嚟喎 'he says he's not coming'.

ex.en: Hey, it's raining!

words.note: 我嘅 = mine. 紅色嘅 = the red one. With family and close things it's often dropped: 我媽媽.

ex.en: Whose phone is this? — It's mine.

words.en: some; the (plural); (after adj) a bit more
words.fr: quelques ; les (pluriel) ; (après adj.) un peu plus
words.note: Three uses: 啲菜 'the vegetables', 飲啲水 'drink some water', 快啲 'faster'.

ex.en: Have some more!

words.note: Always before the verb: 我都係 'me too'. 我哋都 = we all.

ex.en: I like milk tea too.

words.en: again (already happened); 又…又… both … and …
words.fr: encore (déjà arrivé) ; 又…又… à la fois … et …
words.note: 又 = again for something that happened (often with annoyance). 又平又靚 = cheap and pretty.

ex.en: You're late again!

words.note: 再 = do it again later. 再見 = see you again. Compare 又 for the past.

ex.en: Could you say that again?

words.en: first; (end of sentence) first, before anything else
words.note: Before the verb: 我先走 'I'll leave first'. Very Cantonese at the end: 食先 'eat first'.

ex.en: Let's eat first, we'll talk later.

words.note: 就嚟 = coming right now. 噉就 = in that case. 就係 = exactly, that's it.

ex.en: I'm almost there!

words.note: 仲未 = still not. 仲貴 = even more expensive. 仲有 = and also / there's still.

ex.en: He still hasn't got up.

words.en: seems; it looks like; to be like

ex.en: It looks like it's going to rain.

words.fr: ou (dans une question : A ou B ?)
words.note: Only in questions where you choose one. Often shortened to 定.

ex.en: Coffee or tea?

words.note: Either is fine: 聽日或者後日 'tomorrow or the day after'. At the start: 'maybe'.

ex.en: We can take the MTR or the bus.

sentences.en: I ate dim sum yesterday, and I'm eating dim sum again today!
What are you watching? — I'm watching the news.
I've been to Hong Kong, but I haven't been to Macau yet.
Have you eaten? — Not yet.
Did you go to work yesterday? — No, I didn't.
The rain has stopped, let's go out!
Do you want this one or that one?
This one or that one, either is fine.
That restaurant is both cheap and tasty.
Is it still raining? — It's raining even harder!
You seem a bit tired.
I'll go first, see you tomorrow!
As soon as I get home I'll take a shower.
These clothes are my sister's.

grammar.title: Aspect markers: 咗 done, 緊 -ing, 過 ever
grammar.explain: Cantonese verbs don't change for tense. Instead, a marker straight after the verb says how the action stands: 咗 = finished, 緊 = in progress, 過 = has been experienced at some time. The negatives are 冇 + verb (didn't), and 未 + verb + 過 (never yet).

examples.en: I ate / I'm eating / I've eaten it before.
I've been to Japan, but I haven't been to Korea.

grammar.title: Sentence particles: 啊, 啦, 喇, 㗎, 喎
grammar.explain: The last syllable sets the mood. 啊 softens; 啦 suggests or urges ('come on'); 喇 announces a change ('now, already'); 㗎 explains a fact; 喎 passes on news or something you just noticed. 啦 laa1 and 喇 laa3 differ only in tone!

examples.en: The boss says there's no meeting today, apparently.

grammar.title: 定係 vs 或者: two kinds of 'or'
grammar.explain: 定係 asks the listener to choose: 'A or B?' It only appears in questions. 或者 offers options in a statement: 'A or B, either is fine.'

examples.en: Are you going on Saturday or Sunday?
I'll go on Saturday or Sunday.
Hot or iced? — Either is fine.

lines.en: Have you had lunch yet?
Not yet, I'm still writing an email.
It's already one-thirty! Eat first, come on!
OK. Do you want noodles or rice?
Either is fine. Have you been to the new cha chaan teng downstairs?
I went yesterday. It's cheap and good.
Then let's go there again today!
Huh, seems like the boss is coming over…
Quick, let's go, right now!

questions.q: Why hasn't B had lunch yet?
options: B is still writing an email

questions.q: What time is it?
What does B say about the new cha chaan teng?
Why do they hurry off at the end?

units.title: Free Time & Sports
units.desc: Talk about your hobbies, how often you do things, and plan a weekend outing

words.note: Question form: 得唔得閒 dak1 m4 dak1 haan4? 'Are you free?'

ex.en: Are you free this Saturday?
What are your hobbies?

words.fr: aller au cinéma / voir un film
words.note: 戲 = film. Classifier is 套 tou3: 呢套戲 'this film'.

ex.en: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

words.note: Literally 'walk mountain' — Hong Kong's favourite weekend sport.

ex.en: Hong Kong has lots of places to go hiking.
In summer I often go swimming at the beach.

words.note: 打 for ball games played with the hands; for a specific sport say 打籃球 'play basketball'.

ex.en: After school he plays basketball with his classmates.

words.note: 踢 = to kick.

ex.en: My little brother plays football every Sunday.

words.en: to sing; to go to karaoke
words.note: Going to karaoke is usually called 唱K (coeng3 kei1) — the K is the English letter.

ex.en: She sings really well.

words.note: 去旅行 = go on a trip. Note hang4, not haang4 as in 行山.

ex.en: Have you ever been to Japan on a trip?

words.note: One photo = 一張相. 'Take a photo of us' = 幫我哋影張相.

ex.en: Could you take a photo of us, please?
I like listening to music when I take the MTR.
My little brother plays video games all night.

words.note: Everyday word for reading. 讀書 duk6 syu1 means 'to study'.

ex.en: I usually read before going to sleep.

words.note: Literally 'cook things to eat'. 煮飯 also means 'to cook a meal'.

ex.en: At weekends I like cooking at home.

words.note: Also written 周末.

ex.en: What do you usually do at the weekend?

words.en: often, all the time; all day
words.fr: souvent, tout le temps ; toute la journée
words.note: The most common spoken word for 'often'. Context tells you if it means 'all day'.

ex.en: She's always on her phone.

words.note: Same meaning as 成日 but a bit more formal.

ex.en: We often go hiking together.
Sometimes I go to the cinema alone.

words.note: Less often than 有時. Often followed by 都: 間中都會…

ex.en: I do play video games now and then.

words.note: 從來唔 + verb = never do. 從來冇 + verb + 過 = have never (once) done.

ex.en: I never eat spicy food.

words.note: To exercise = 做運動.

ex.en: Do you usually do any exercise?

words.note: 玩 here is waan2 (rising tone).

ex.en: Hiking is great fun!

words.note: Literally 'go to the street' — any going out of the house.

ex.en: It's raining, I don't want to go out.

sentences.en: At weekends I usually go hiking with friends.
What do you like doing in your free time?
I never play video games, but my little brother plays all the time.
It rained yesterday, so we didn't go hiking — we played games at home.
We occasionally go to karaoke after work.
Summer is too hot — I just want to go swimming at the beach.
Do you prefer playing football or basketball?
Sometimes I listen to music before going to sleep.
It's so beautiful here — take a photo of me!
He says he has no time to exercise, but he plays games all night.
Cooking is fun, but washing the dishes is boring.
I haven't read a book in ages.
This film is really good — have you seen it yet?
I've never been to Japan, but I really want to go.

grammar.title: How often: 成日 · 有時 · 間中 · 從來唔
grammar.explain: Frequency words go after the subject (and after any time word), right before the verb. 會 'would, tend to' often follows them.

examples.en: At weekends I often go swimming.

grammar.title: 去 + activity
grammar.explain: To 'go and do' something, put 去 straight before the activity — no extra word for 'to'. Ask with 去唔去.

grammar.title: …嘅時候 = when…
grammar.explain: Put 嘅時候 after a phrase to say 'when / while…'. It comes first, then the main sentence.

examples.en: When I'm free I like to cook.
When I was little I played football all the time.

lines.en: Hey, are you free this Saturday?
I'm free. What's the plan?
How about we go hiking on the Dragon's Back?
Sure! I've never been. Is it a hard walk?
Not hard, it's only about two hours of walking.
So what time do we set off?
Let's meet at Shau Kei Wan station at nine.
Nine?! So early! At weekends I usually don't get up till eleven!
If we go early the sun isn't as strong, and the photos are nicer too.
Fine, fine. I'll bring my camera!

questions.q: Where do they plan to go hiking?
How long is the walk, according to A?
What time does B usually get up at weekends?
Why does A want to start early?
options: The sun is less strong and photos are nicer
A has to work in the afternoon

units.title: Health & Body
units.desc: Say what hurts, describe a cold or fever, and get through a visit to the doctor

words.note: 身體好 = in good health. 身體健康 is a common wish.

ex.en: My grandpa is in very good health.
My head feels a bit dizzy.

words.note: 肚餓 = hungry; 肚痛 = stomach ache.

ex.en: I ate too much, my stomach is so full.
Wash your hands before eating.
I walked all day, my feet are killing me.

words.note: Many people say 'aan5' without ng-.

ex.en: I've been looking at the computer all day, my eyes are tired.
My throat is a bit sore.
Where does it hurt?

words.fr: mal de tête ; avoir mal à la tête

ex.en: I've had a headache since this morning.
I ate seafood last night and now my stomach hurts.
Have you got a fever? Your face is very red.
He's been coughing for a week.

words.en: cold / flu; to catch a cold
words.note: Also: 傷風 soeng1 fung1 (a common cold). Catching a chill = 凍親.

ex.en: I've caught a cold, I've got a runny nose.

words.note: Literally 'flow nose water'.

ex.en: The doctor says it's nothing serious.
If you're still coughing, go and see a doctor.
There's a clinic downstairs from my place.

words.note: 院 is jyun2 here (rising tone).

ex.en: My grandma is in hospital.
The doctor prescribed me two kinds of medicine.

words.note: In Cantonese you 'eat' medicine — even liquid medicine.

ex.en: Have you taken your medicine yet?
You should rest for a couple of days.

words.note: 攞病假 lo2 beng6 gaa3 = take sick leave.

ex.en: I'm taking a day of sick leave today.

words.note: 返 after an adjective = back to a normal state.

ex.en: Have you got better?
The floor is slippery, be careful!

sentences.en: I don't feel well today, I don't want to go to work.
You have a fever — go and see the doctor quickly.
My throat hurts and I keep coughing.
Take this medicine three times a day, after meals.
I've caught a cold, so I'm not going hiking tomorrow.
Drink more water and rest well.
Is the hospital far from here?
He fell playing football and hurt his foot.
Mind your hands, the stove is very hot!
Are you feeling better? — Much better, thanks.
I've had a headache all day — maybe I'm too tired.
I rarely take medicine — I usually just sleep and get better.
Can I take a day of sick leave tomorrow?

grammar.title: Body part + 痛
grammar.explain: To say something hurts, put 痛 after the body part. A classifier like 個 / 隻 / 對 before the body part sounds very natural: 我個頭好痛.

examples.en: My left foot hurts a bit.

grammar.title: 有啲 + adjective = a bit (unpleasant)
grammar.explain: 有啲 before an adjective means 'a bit / somewhat', usually for something negative. Compare 啲 after an adjective, which means '-er': 好啲 'better'.

grammar.title: Verb + 返 = back to normal
grammar.explain: 返 after an adjective or verb means returning to the normal state: 好返 'get well again', 瞓返 'go back to sleep'.

examples.en: I woke up at three and couldn't get back to sleep.

lines.en: Hello, where are you feeling unwell?
Doctor, my throat has been very sore since yesterday, and I keep coughing.
Do you have a fever?
A little. Last night it was thirty-eight degrees.
Open your mouth and let me have a look... It's a bit inflamed. You've caught a cold.
Is it serious? I have a football match on Saturday.
Not serious. But you'd better rest for two days — no football this week.
Oh no... Then can you write me a sick note?
Sure. Take this medicine three times a day, after meals, and drink more water.
Thank you, doctor!

questions.q: What are B's symptoms?
options: Sore throat, cough and a slight fever
Sore eyes and a runny nose

questions.q: What does the doctor say B has?
Why is B worried?
options: B has a football match on Saturday
B is going on a trip

questions.q: How should B take the medicine?
options: Three times a day after meals

units.title: Work & Study
units.desc: Talk about your job, colleagues, school and exams — and survive a job interview

words.note: 返公司 = go to the office.

ex.en: Which company do you work for?

words.note: Very colloquial alternative: 老細 lou5 sai3.

ex.en: My boss is very nice.
I have lunch with my colleagues every day.

words.note: 份 is the classifier for jobs. 工作 gung1 zok3 is the more formal word.

ex.en: Do you like your job?

words.note: Used in more formal speech or writing, e.g. 工作經驗 'work experience'. Day to day, people say 做嘢 or 返工.

ex.en: Do you have any work experience?

words.note: 會 is wui2 here (rising tone).

ex.en: Sorry, I'm in a meeting, I'll call you back later.
I have to work overtime again tonight.

words.note: Send an email = 寄電郵 / 發電郵.

ex.en: Have you read the email I sent you?
She's been looking for a job for three months.
I have an interview tomorrow morning, I'm so nervous.

words.note: 加人工 = get a raise.

ex.en: The pay at this job isn't bad.
He quit because he was too busy.

words.en: to be on holiday / day off

ex.en: When are you on holiday?
I've been really busy lately, no time to go hiking.

words.en: to study; to go to school
words.note: 你讀緊書？ = Are you still a student?

ex.en: Are you working or still studying?
I've been learning Cantonese for a year.
There are lots of students in the library.

words.note: Address a teacher as surname + 老師, e.g. 陳老師.

ex.en: Our teacher speaks very fast.
I have an exam next week, I need to revise.

words.en: to revise, study for an exam

ex.en: Have you finished your homework?

words.note: Question: 明唔明白? Short reply: 明白 / 明.

ex.en: Do you understand what I mean?
Sorry, I don't understand. Could you say it again?
Teacher, I have a question.

sentences.en: I'm so busy at work that I don't even have time for lunch.
The boss is in a meeting, come back in an hour.
Have you replied to that email yet?
I worked overtime until eleven last night, I'm exhausted.
My colleague quit, so I have to do her work.
When I'm on holiday I don't want to read any work emails.
I don't understand this question, can you teach me?
The teacher gave us lots of homework again today.
Did the exam go well? — Not bad, I think I'll pass.
She studied in England, so her English is very good.
The pay is good, but I have to work overtime every day.
Since I came to Geneva, I've been learning French.
Is your company big?

grammar.title: Verb + 到 + result = so … that
grammar.explain: Put 到 after an adjective or verb, then say the result: 忙到冇時間食飯 'so busy I have no time to eat'.

examples.en: I'm so tired I can't open my eyes.
He was so happy he jumped up.

grammar.title: Splitting verb + object: 辭咗職, 讀過書
grammar.explain: Many two-character verbs are really verb + object (辭職, 讀書, 開會, 搵工). Aspect markers and durations go in the middle: 開緊會, 辭咗職, 搵咗三個月工.

examples.en: I studied for four years at university.

grammar.title: 因為…所以… = because … so …
grammar.explain: Unlike English, Cantonese happily uses both halves together. You can also drop either one.

examples.en: Because I have an exam, I'm not going out tonight.
Why did you quit? — Because the pay was too low.

lines.en: Please have a seat. Could you introduce yourself first?
Sure. I'm Wing, I studied design at university.
Do you have any work experience?
I worked at an advertising company for three years.
Then why do you want to change jobs?
Over there I had to work overtime every day, till midnight — I want to learn new things.
Ha, we're not that busy here. Do you have any questions?
Um... about how much is the pay?
Let's talk about pay in the second interview. We'll email you next week.
Great, thank you very much!

questions.q: What did Wing study at university?
How long did Wing work at the advertising company?
Why does Wing want to change jobs?
options: Too much overtime; wants to learn new things

questions.q: How will Wing hear back?

units.title: Making Plans
units.desc: Suggest plans, fix a time and place, reschedule, and explain why you're running late

words.en: to arrange to meet; an appointment
words.note: 我約咗人 = I'm meeting someone. 有約 = I have plans.

ex.en: I've arranged to meet a friend for dinner on Friday.

words.note: Split it to add a time: 見過面, 見一次面.

ex.en: We haven't met up in ages!

words.note: 不如 … 啦 is the standard way to suggest something.

ex.en: How about we go and eat hotpot?
Good idea! I haven't had hotpot in ages.

words.en: is that OK? / does that work?
words.note: Answer 得 (OK) or 唔得 (no, can't).

ex.en: Seven-thirty, does that work for you?

words.note: Same as 得閒; 有空 sounds slightly more polite.

ex.en: When are you free next week?

words.note: Also used for meeting points: 喺門口等 'meet (wait) at the entrance'.

ex.en: Where shall we meet?
Sorry, I'm going to be late by ten minutes.
He's never on time.
Can we make it a bit earlier?
I'm busy now, let's talk later.

words.en: in a moment; a little while
words.note: 一陣見 = see you in a bit. 等一陣 = wait a moment.

ex.en: OK, see you in a bit!
There's a typhoon, the event's been cancelled.
Can we reschedule to next week?
Sorry, something came up at the last minute, I can't come.

words.note: 記得 + verb = remember to do.

ex.en: Remember to bring an umbrella.

words.note: 唔記得咗 = have forgotten.

ex.en: Oops, I forgot we had plans today!

words.note: 打電話畀我 = call me.

ex.en: Call me when you get there.

words.note: 傳訊息 / 發訊息 = send a message. In real life most people just say the English 'WhatsApp'.

ex.en: I sent you a message, did you get it?
Why haven't you replied to me?

words.note: 我就嚟到 = I'm almost there. 就嚟 + verb = about to.

ex.en: Don't worry, I'm almost there!
Let's meet at the cinema entrance.

sentences.en: Are you free tomorrow night? How about we go to the movies?
What time shall we meet, and where?
The film starts at eight, let's meet at seven-thirty.
Sorry, I have to work overtime tonight — can we reschedule?
It's a typhoon tomorrow, the hike will probably be cancelled.
He's late again — we've been waiting for half an hour!
Remember to send me a message when you leave.
I forgot to bring my phone, so I couldn't call you.
Is Saturday afternoon OK? — No, I already have plans.
Let's meet up for a meal again some other time.
Wait for me a moment, I'm just coming down.
Why don't we go a bit earlier, there are fewer people.
Did he reply to you? — Not yet.

grammar.title: 不如…啦 = how about…
grammar.explain: Start with 不如 and end with 啦 to make a friendly suggestion. To accept: 好啊 / 好主意; to decline politely: 唔得啊，我約咗人.

examples.en: How about meeting at the MTR station?
How about we reschedule to Sunday?

grammar.title: Time + place + verb
grammar.explain: Cantonese order is fixed: who → when → where → what. 我哋 + 七點 + 喺門口 + 等.

examples.en: We'll meet at seven at the entrance.
Tomorrow I'm having lunch with a colleague in Central.

grammar.title: Verb + 唔到 = can't manage to
grammar.explain: 唔到 after a verb means you tried or wanted to but couldn't: 嚟唔到 'can't make it', 搵唔到 'can't find'.

examples.en: Sorry, I can't make it tonight.
I can't find you — where are you?

lines.en: We haven't met up in ages! How about hotpot this Friday?
Good idea! But I might have to work overtime on Friday...
Then let's make it Saturday night. Does eight o'clock work?
Works for me. Where shall we meet?
Outside Langham Place in Mong Kok. Don't be late this time!
Relax, I'll definitely be on time!
(Saturday, 8:20) Hey, where are you? I've been waiting twenty minutes!
Sorry, sorry! I forgot to bring my Octopus card and had to go home to get it...
You said you'd definitely be on time!
I'm almost there, five more minutes! Dinner's on me tonight, OK?

questions.q: Why can't B do Friday?
options: B might have to work overtime

questions.q: Where and when do they agree to meet?
options: Langham Place in Mong Kok, Saturday at 8
Langham Place in Mong Kok, Friday at 8

questions.q: Why is B late?
options: B forgot the Octopus card and went home to get it

questions.q: How does B try to make up for being late?

units.title: Opinions & Comparing
units.desc: Give your opinion, compare two things, agree and disagree — politely or not

words.note: The everyday way to give an opinion: 我覺得… 'I think…'.

ex.en: What do you think of this restaurant?

words.note: More formal than 覺得 — meetings, news, debates.

ex.en: I believe this plan isn't feasible.

words.fr: par rapport à (A 比 B + adj)
words.note: A 比 B 平 = A is cheaper than B. Same sound as 畀 'give' — different character.

ex.en: Hong Kong is hotter than Geneva.

words.note: The most colloquial comparison: 我高過你 'I'm taller than you'. Not the same as the aspect 過 'have ever'.

ex.en: The MTR is faster than the bus.

words.note: 最 + adjective/verb: 最平 the cheapest, 最鍾意 like best.

ex.en: Which restaurant do you like best?
Eating at home is better than eating out.

words.note: A 冇 B 咁 + adj = A is not as … as B.

ex.en: Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
The two restaurants are about the same price.

words.note: A 同 B 一樣 = A is the same as B.

ex.en: My phone is the same as yours.
What's the difference between these two?
I like Hong Kong because the food is great.

words.note: Pairs with 但係: 雖然…但係… 'although…, (but)…'.

ex.en: Although it's expensive, it's really good.

words.note: Softer than 但係; very common at the start of a sentence.

ex.en: It's tasty, but the portions are a bit small.
Actually, I don't like spicy food much.
You should try their milk tea.
Maybe it'll rain this afternoon.
You'll definitely like it!
Expensive isn't necessarily good.
I don't agree with you.

words.note: 你講得啱 = you're right. 啱啱 ngaam1 ngaam1 = just now.

ex.en: You're right, it's much cheaper here.

words.note: 唔錯 = not bad (actually means 'good'). 冇錯 = exactly, that's right.

ex.en: Sorry, I took the wrong bus.

words.note: 抵食 = good value food. Very HK!

ex.en: This set meal is only forty dollars, such good value!
What's your opinion?

sentences.en: I think Hong Kong summers are hotter than Geneva's.
Taking the MTR is more convenient than taking a taxi, and cheaper too.
Which is the best cha chaan teng in Hong Kong?
Although Cantonese is hard, I think it's very interesting.
Because it's raining, I'd rather stay at home.
Actually the two phones are almost the same, only the colour is different.
This shirt isn't as nice as that one.
You should go and see a doctor — you might have a fever.
He's definitely going to be late again.
Do you agree? — I agree, but my boss might not.
Sorry, I said it wrong — it's Thursday, not Tuesday.
Is hiking better, or swimming? — I prefer swimming.
My job is busier than before, but the pay is the same.

grammar.title: Comparing: A + adj + 過 + B
grammar.explain: The most natural spoken comparison: adjective then 過 then the thing compared. 比 also works (A 比 B + adj) but sounds a bit more formal. 'Much more' = add 好多 at the end.

examples.en: I'm taller than my big brother.
Hong Kong is much more expensive than Geneva? Not necessarily!
This one is cheaper than that one.

grammar.title: A 冇 B 咁 + adj = not as … as
grammar.explain: To say A is less … than B, use 冇 and 咁.

examples.en: Swimming isn't as tiring as hiking.
My Cantonese isn't as good as yours.

grammar.title: Verb + 多啲 = prefer
grammar.explain: 鍾意 X 多啲 means 'I like X more'. 多啲 goes after the object, at the end.

examples.en: Do you prefer dogs or cats?

dialogue.title: Cha chaan teng vs. the new ramen place

lines.en: What shall we have for lunch? How about that new ramen place?
Ramen again? I think the cha chaan teng downstairs is better than ramen.
The cha chaan teng is so noisy, and the waiters are so rude!
But it's cheap! A set meal is forty dollars, with milk tea included — such good value.
The ramen is a bit more expensive, but the place is nicer and you can take photos.
Are you going to eat or take photos? The queue there takes at least an hour!
...You're right. We only have an hour for lunch.
So — cha chaan teng today, ramen on Saturday?
Deal! But on Saturday you're paying!

questions.q: Which restaurant does B prefer?
options: B wants to cook at home

questions.q: What does A dislike about the cha chaan teng?
options: It's noisy and the waiters are rude

questions.q: Why does A finally agree with B?
options: The ramen queue is at least an hour and lunch is only an hour

questions.q: What is the final plan?
options: Cha chaan teng today, ramen on Saturday
Ramen today, cha chaan teng on Saturday

units.title: Telling Stories
units.desc: Tell what happened: set the scene, move the story on, and deliver the twist

words.note: Used for general past habits: 我以前… 'I used to…'.

ex.en: I used to work in Hong Kong.

words.note: Goes AFTER the event: 食飯之前 = before eating. 三年之前 = three years ago.

ex.en: Wash your hands before eating.

words.note: Very common in spoken storytelling, more colloquial than 然後.

ex.en: I'll go to the bank first, then go grocery shopping.
In the end he still didn't come.

words.note: Carries relief: something you waited for finally happened.

ex.en: I've finally found a job!

words.note: Marks a discovery: 'oh, so that's how it is'.

ex.en: So you can speak Cantonese!
Suddenly the power went out and everything went dark.

words.note: 啱啱 + verb = just did. Alone, 啱啱好 = just right.

ex.en: He just left — you missed him by a step.

words.en: all along; the whole time; while
words.note: 一路 A 一路 B = doing A while doing B.

ex.en: He listens to music while he drives.

words.note: A bit more formal than 嗰陣.

ex.en: At the time I didn't know he was the boss.

words.note: Also 嗰陣時. Put it after a clause: 我讀書嗰陣 = when I was studying.

ex.en: When I was a student I loved playing ball.
What happened just now? Why are there so many police?

words.note: An event you went through, not work experience (that's 經驗).

ex.en: This is the most unforgettable experience of my life.
Grandma often tells me stories about the old days.

words.en: as a result; in the end
words.note: Introduces the (often bad) outcome.

ex.en: He didn't revise, so in the end he failed the exam.

words.note: Sets up a plan that then changed.

ex.en: I was originally going to go, but something came up.

words.note: Only for the past. For the future say 遲啲.

ex.en: Later on they got married.

words.note: The twist word: 'I expected X, but then…'.

ex.en: I thought it would be sunny, but then it rained all day.

words.note: Shows surprise or disbelief.

ex.en: He actually forgot his own birthday!

words.note: Classic story opener.

ex.en: Once I fell asleep on the MTR and missed my stop.
When he got the news he rushed over immediately.

words.note: 差啲 + bad thing = it almost happened (but didn't).

ex.en: I overslept this morning and was almost late.

sentences.en: I used to live in Kowloon; later I moved to Hong Kong Island.
Do you remember what happened when we first met?
I had just stepped out the door when it suddenly started pouring.
We'd planned to go hiking, but a typhoon came, so we had to cancel.
I always thought she was Japanese — turns out she's Korean.
I was so nervous at the time that I nearly failed the exam.
We waited half an hour and the bus finally came.
After hearing the news, he immediately phoned his family.
Back then I'd just graduated and didn't know a thing.
And then what happened? Hurry up and finish the story!
That experience made me realise that health matters more than money.
In the end we decided not to go and had hotpot at home.
When I was little I was afraid of the dark and had to sleep with the light on.
I actually bumped into my primary-school classmate in Geneva — who'd have guessed!

grammar.title: 本來… 點知… — the plan and the twist
grammar.explain: 本來 sets up what was supposed to happen; 點知 ('who knew') brings in what actually happened. It's the backbone of most Cantonese anecdotes.

examples.en: I was going to go hiking, but then it rained.
I thought he wouldn't come — turns out he was first to arrive.

grammar.title: Clause + 嗰陣 = 'when …'
grammar.explain: To say 'when X happened', put the whole clause first and end it with 嗰陣 (or 嗰陣時). There's no word at the front like English 'when'.

examples.en: When I was little I lived in New Zealand.
When I got home, he was already asleep.

grammar.title: 一路 A 一路 B — doing two things at once
grammar.explain: Repeat 一路 before each verb: 一路行一路食 = eat while walking. On its own, 一路 means 'all along' (我一路以為…).

lines.en: Once, I took a minibus home from Mong Kok after work.
I was really tired then, and soon after sitting down I fell asleep.
Suddenly the driver shouted that we'd reached the terminus, and I jumped up and got off.
Not long after getting off, I realised my wallet was gone!
Inside were my ID card and a few hundred dollars in cash.
I ran straight back to the terminus, but the minibus had already left.
At the time I really didn't know what to do, so I just went to the police station to report it.
I'd assumed I'd never get the wallet back.
But then the next morning, an old man phoned me.
It turned out he'd picked up my wallet on the minibus.
He found my business card inside, so he knew whom to call.
He even came all the way out from Tuen Mun just to give it back to me.
I opened it and — amazingly — not a single dollar was missing!
I wanted to give him some money to say thanks, but he just smiled and said there was no need.
In the end I treated him to a milk tea, and we chatted while we drank.
That experience made me feel Hong Kong really is full of human warmth.

questions.q: Where did the narrator most likely lose the wallet?
How did the old man know whom to contact?
options: He found a business card in the wallet
He saw the narrator's name on the ID card
The police gave him the number

questions.q: What did the narrator expect after reporting the loss?
options: That the wallet would never come back
That the police would call the next day
That the driver would keep it
That only the cash would be missing

questions.q: Why does the story end with the narrator praising Hong Kong?
options: A stranger went out of his way and refused a reward
The police found the wallet quickly
The narrator found extra money in the wallet

units.title: Advanced Patterns
units.desc: Link ideas like a native: passives, 'even', 'as soon as', 'the more… the more', 'even if', 'rather'

words.note: 畀 + doer + verb: 畀人偷咗 = got stolen (by someone). Cantonese must name a doer; use 人 if unknown.

ex.en: My bike got stolen.

words.note: 將 + object + verb + where: moves the object before the verb. Slightly formal; very common in instructions.

ex.en: Please take the rubbish downstairs.

words.note: Put the surprising item between 連 and 都.

ex.en: He's so busy he doesn't even have time to eat.

words.note: 一 + first action, 就 + second action.

ex.en: I go home as soon as I finish work.

words.note: 越嚟越 + adjective or 鍾意 etc.

ex.en: The weather is getting hotter and hotter.

words.note: 越 + verb, 越 + result.

ex.en: The more he talked, the angrier he got.

words.note: Often followed by 仲 (also) or 都 (all).

ex.en: Besides Cantonese, he can also speak French.

words.note: 就 goes after the subject in the second clause.

ex.en: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go hiking.

words.note: A minimum condition that is enough.

ex.en: As long as you practise, you'll definitely learn it.

words.note: 就算 + condition, (subject) 都 + result.

ex.en: Even if there's a typhoon tomorrow, I still have to work.

words.note: Usually with a question word: 無論幾貴 / 無論邊個.

ex.en: No matter how expensive, she wants to buy it.

words.note: 寧願 A，都唔 B = I'd rather A than B. Often said ning4 jyun2 in fast speech.

ex.en: I'd rather take the stairs than squeeze into the lift.

words.en: no need to; don't have to

ex.en: No need to wait for me, I'm working late tonight.
When you come to Hong Kong you must try egg tarts.

words.note: Adds impatience to a question.

ex.en: What on earth do you want?

words.note: Like 到底, a bit more neutral.

ex.en: Who exactly ate all the cake?

words.note: Result is the opposite of what you'd expect.

ex.en: He didn't get angry — instead he burst out laughing.

words.note: Raises the stakes; a bit more formal than 連…都.

ex.en: He loves Japan so much he even taught himself Japanese.
Hurry up, otherwise we won't make it.

words.note: A 先至 B = only after A can B. Shorter: 先.

ex.en: Only after finishing your homework can you play video games.

words.note: Before a verb or noun.

ex.en: I only had a coffee, I haven't eaten.
Getting to the airport from here takes at least an hour.

sentences.en: My phone got stolen — I can't even get back the photos on it.
As soon as she heard the news she burst into tears.
If you forgot your umbrella, just buy one at the convenience store.
Apart from Sunday, he has to work every day.
Do you actually know what you did wrong or not?
I'd rather cook myself than eat takeaway every day.
As long as it doesn't rain, we'll go for a beach barbecue tomorrow.
He likes Hong Kong more and more, and is even thinking of moving there.
Even if you failed the exam, there's no need to be so upset.
Please give this document to the boss — he needs to see it as soon as he's back.
The older the kid gets, the more he looks like his dad.
You're all talk — when exactly are you going to actually do it?
No matter how busy he is, he calls home every week.

grammar.title: Passive with 畀
grammar.explain: Cantonese passive is 'thing + 畀 + doer + verb (+咗)'. Unlike English, the doer can't be dropped: if you don't know who, say 畀人. It's mostly used for unpleasant events.

examples.en: I got told off by the boss.
His wallet was stolen by someone.
The cake got eaten by my little brother.

grammar.title: 就 in the second half
grammar.explain: 一…就 (as soon as), 如果…就 (if), 只要…就 (as long as) all put 就 right before the verb of the second clause — after its subject, never before it.

examples.en: As soon as I get home I take a shower.
As long as you're happy, that's fine.

grammar.title: 就算 / 無論 … 都
grammar.explain: Concessive clauses take 都 in the second half: 'even if X, (subject) still Y'. 寧願 A 都唔 B works the same way: 'rather A than B'.

examples.en: Even if it rains, I'm still going.
No matter what you say, he won't listen.

lines.en: Why do you look so tired today?
Sigh, I get woken up every morning by the renovation next door — not even Saturday is spared.
How long on earth do they still need?
They say at least two months. The more I think about it, the angrier I get.
Have you complained to the management office?
I have, but management says as long as they don't work at night, there's nothing they can do.
Then why don't you come and stay at my place for a while? I've got a spare room.
Thanks, but I'd rather put up with it for two months than trouble you.
No need to be polite! Even if you stayed half a year, I wouldn't mind.
Really? Then besides paying the electricity, I can also cook and tidy up for you!
Great! If you're willing to cook, I should be the one thanking you.
It's a deal! I'll pack my stuff and come over as soon as I finish work tonight.
Remember to bring a pillow and blanket — that room only has a bed.

questions.q: Why is B so tired?
options: The neighbours' renovation wakes B up every morning
B was out late on Saturday

questions.q: What did the management office say?
options: They can't stop it as long as the work isn't at night
The work will finish in two weeks
B should complain to the police
The renovation is not allowed on Saturdays

questions.q: Why did B first turn down A's offer?
options: B didn't want to be a burden

questions.q: What can we infer about the spare room?
options: It's mostly empty apart from a bed

units.title: HK Slang & Colloquial
units.desc: Sound like a local with everyday (clean) slang — and know when it fits

words.note: Casual but fine at work. 搞唔掂 = can't handle it.

ex.en: Don't worry, I'll sort this out for you.

words.note: 掂唔掂啊? = Is it going OK? Casual.

ex.en: How's your new job going — all good?

words.note: Slang reading zeng3 (the standard reading zing3 means 'upright'). Casual, very common for food.

ex.en: The milk tea here is fantastic!

words.note: A warm compliment, often for kids or juniors.

ex.en: His son is really smart — he knows to help out.

words.note: As an adverb: 求其揀 = just pick any. As criticism: 做嘢好求其 = careless.

ex.en: Just pick any one, we're in a hurry.

words.en: can't stand it; can't take it
words.note: Venting, informal. 頂得順 = can bear it.

ex.en: My colleague talks loudly on the phone all day — I can't stand it.

words.note: An exclamation of joy. Not 'good things'.

ex.en: Yay! Tomorrow's a holiday!

words.note: Reply to 你冇嘢吖嘛? (You OK?). Also 'nothing at all'.

ex.en: I'm fine, just a bit tired.

words.en: knock off (work); call it a day
words.note: More casual than 放工; also said when finishing any task.

ex.en: What time do you knock off?

words.note: 好抵 = great deal. 抵食 = good-value food. 唔抵 = not worth it.

ex.en: This top is only a hundred dollars after the discount — what a deal!

words.en: get shot down; hit a wall
words.note: Literally 'bump into a board'. When a request is flatly refused.

ex.en: I asked the boss for leave and got shot down.

words.note: Literally 'the chicken ran off'.

ex.en: Buy one get one free today — don't miss out!

words.note: 我講笑咋 = I'm only joking.

ex.en: Don't be cross, I was only joking with you.

words.note: Opposite of 求其. 講笑定認真? = joking or serious?

ex.en: She works very conscientiously — she's never sloppy.

words.note: Describes the situation, not you: 真係激氣! = how infuriating!

ex.en: I've waited half an hour and the bus still hasn't come — so annoying!

words.note: 好彩…唔係嘅話… = luckily…otherwise…

ex.en: Luckily you reminded me, otherwise I'd definitely have forgotten.

words.note: Mild, teasing; fine with friends but rude to strangers or elders.

ex.en: Are you nuts? Going hiking in this heavy rain!

words.note: Surprise or admiration; can also show shock.

ex.en: Wow, your home is beautiful!

words.note: Literally 'big wok'. 大鑊喇! = We're in trouble!

ex.en: Uh-oh! I forgot to bring my passport!

words.en: to chat idly; shoot the breeze
words.note: Also 'to talk big'. 吹下水 = have a chat.

ex.en: We chatted all evening and before we knew it, it was midnight.

words.note: Easy-going reply when given a choice. Can sound careless in formal settings.

ex.en: I'm easy, whatever you want to eat is fine.

words.note: Said of someone who agreed to come and then didn't.

ex.en: He always says he'll come, and always bails.

words.en: fall for a trap; get ripped off
words.note: For tourist traps, bad buys, overhyped restaurants.

ex.en: That restaurant was expensive and awful — we got had.

words.note: Handling a surprise on the spot. Positive: 識執生 = resourceful.

ex.en: He wasn't prepared but spoke really well — he knows how to wing it.

words.note: For meeting again later the same day.

ex.en: I'm heading out now, see you soon!

words.note: Outraged disbelief. Strong but not vulgar.

ex.en: Are you kidding me? An hour's wait and still no table!

sentences.en: Everything's sorted — I can finally call it a day!
The set meal at this cha chaan teng is under fifty dollars — real value.
The new colleague is sharp — you only have to show him once.
Don't be so sloppy, otherwise you'll have to clean up the mess again.
Wow, you've had a haircut? Looks great!
It's unbearably hot today, I really don't want to go out.
Luckily I brought an umbrella, otherwise I'd be soaked.
He's made plans with me three times and bailed all three — so infuriating!
The concert tickets sold out the moment they went on sale — I missed out again.
I was only joking, but he took it seriously.
Are you kidding? A bowl of wonton noodles for a whole hundred dollars!
After work we went to a cha chaan teng for a chat.
You're OK, right? You look a bit pale.

grammar.title: Can / can't: verb + 得 / 唔 + result
grammar.explain: Many slang verbs have a result part. Put 得 in the middle for 'can', 唔 for 'can't': 搞得掂 / 搞唔掂, 頂得順 / 頂唔順. Questions use 唔 twice: 頂唔頂得順?

examples.en: I can't handle this on my own.
Don't worry, I can handle it.

grammar.title: Flavour particles: 喎, 咋, 吖嘛
grammar.explain: Slang lives in the particles. 喎 wo3 = 'hey, I notice…' or passing on what someone said. 咋 zaa3 = 'only, that's all'. 吖嘛 aa1 maa3 = 'right? / you know' (checking or stating the obvious).
